stops.name: Brussels, the house of the silk merchant
stops.campa: Charlotte Bachrach is born on 20 April in Brussels, daughter of Paul Bachrach, a German-Jewish silk merchant grown wealthy in the fabric trade, and of his wife Elvira. The house is no ordinary merchant's house: Heinrich Vogeler of Worpswede, master of the Jugendstil, has a hand in its rooms, so the child opens her eyes among drawn lilies and stained light. Silk, the moth's thread, is the family element; the daughter will spend her life making cloth move like spirit.

stops.name: Brussels, the first lessons with Jeanne Defaw
stops.campa: At six years old Charlotte is given to Jeanne Defaw, a Belgian pupil of Isadora Duncan, and the barefoot gospel enters her body before any other creed. Defaw teaches the Duncan liberty: no barre, no blocked shoe, the arm lifted as the soul lifts, and the grave little girl takes to it not as play but as devotion. Watchers already note the strange stillness of her face when she moves, as of a child listening to something in the next room.

stops.name: Brussels, the stone saints of Sainte-Gudule
stops.campa: In the cathedral of Saint Michael and Saint Gudula the girl stands before the stone saints and finds the alphabet she will spend her life spelling: the long praying hands, the grave inclined head, the body folded like a wing. From the Gothic sculptors and the Flemish painters of heaven she takes her whole grammar: not steps but attitudes of the soul. Years later the Berlin critics will say she discovered the soul of the Gothic entirely for herself; it is here that it discovers her.

stops.name: Brussels, the war takes the house
stops.campa: On 20 August the German army enters Brussels. The Bachrachs, German Jews in a Belgian capital at war with Germany, are suddenly enemies in their own house: the property is confiscated, the silk business seized, and the family must go. Charlotte, thirteen, leaves the city of Defaw's lessons and the stone saints with what can be carried. The war that unhouses her also delivers her, for the road of exile runs north to a painter's hill she will remember as a refuge.

stops.name: Worpswede, the Barkenhoff of Heinrich Vogeler
stops.campa: Charlotte and her mother come to rest at the Barkenhoff, Heinrich Vogeler's birch-hung house at Worpswede on the moor above Bremen: the family's old friend, the artist of their Brussels rooms, now their shelter. The colony of painters takes the grave Belgian child in among its canvases and peat-black canals. In the enormous northern light she goes on dancing, teaching herself, working the Gothic attitudes into a discipline no school gives her. Vogeler will paint her portrait; the moor keeps her; the war stays outside the birches.

stops.name: Brussels, the debut of the sixteen-year-old
stops.campa: In 1917, in occupied Brussels, Charlotte gives her first public evening of dances. She is sixteen. The city of her childhood, hungry and garrisoned, watches a girl perform grave sacred attitudes out of the thirteenth century as though the cathedral porch had stepped down and begun to move. It is a strange debut, wartime, a borrowed hall, an audience wrapped in coats, and it is remembered as the beginning: from this night she is a dancer publicly, and the family's ruin has produced its answer.

stops.name: Worpswede: Carl Weidemeyer, the builder to come
stops.campa: At Worpswede in 1918 the Bachrachs meet Carl Weidemeyer of Bremen, painter and graphic artist of the colony, not yet an architect. Nothing is built; everything is founded. Ten years on, this acquaintance of the moor will raise for Charlotte the white temple of dance at Ascona, the first modern chamber theater in Switzerland. The canon loves such seeds: on the same birch hill, in the last year of the war, the dancer, her patron father and her future architect stand for a moment in one room.

stops.name: Rotterdam, the Dutch evenings
stops.campa: With the Armistice the borders open and Charlotte carries her dances into the Netherlands, giving evenings at Rotterdam and then Amsterdam through the winter. The Dutch, connoisseurs of the devotional image, receive the gothic dances warmly: the death-dance attitudes, the Egyptian friezes set moving, the praying figures that seem stepped down from an altarpiece. She is seventeen and touring on her own name. The critics reach for painters, not dancers, to describe her: a living sculpture, a panel come down from the altar and walking.

stops.name: The Hague: Raden Mas Jodjana, the hand-language
stops.campa: In Holland she finds the second of her masters: Raden Mas Jodjana, the Javanese prince, in her own estimation the finest mystical dancer alive. From him she learns the language of hands: the fingers as syllables, the wrist as breath, the gesture that speaks without translating. It is the East laid beside her Gothic and found to be the same tongue: dance as worship, the body as temple furniture. Later Uday Shankar, pioneer of the modern dance of India, will complete the oriental initiation.
stops.quote_source: Bara's recorded estimation of Jodjana, cited in the Dizionario della musica nella Svizzera italiana

stops.name: Amsterdam, the acclaim
stops.campa: Amsterdam confirms Rotterdam: full houses for the girl who dances saints. In these Dutch seasons the repertory that will carry her through Europe takes form: Vanité des Vanités, the Danse macabre, the mummy's dance, the Egyptian dance, the Hindu vision, the dying butterfly, each one a memento mori performed with the tenderness of a nun arranging flowers. The Netherlands, which schooled her in Jodjana's East, now sends her out as a name. Berlin is the next altar.

stops.name: Berlin, Max Reinhardt's Kammerspiele
stops.campa: Despite her youth she dances at the Kammerspiele of the Deutsches Theater, Max Reinhardt's chamber stage, and the Berlin critics, the hardest congregation in Europe, are won. In the capital of the new Ausdruckstanz, where Laban's pupils and Wigman's daimon are remaking the body, this Belgian girl arrives from a different century altogether, offering the twelfth. The press names her die gotische Tänzerin, the gothic dancer, and the name holds for life. Berlin will be her northern pole for a decade, with the Theater im Landwehrkasino following in 1920.

stops.name: Berlin: Kolbe's portfolio, Meyer's little book
stops.campa: The sculptors claim her, as she claimed sculpture. Georg Kolbe, master of the dancing bronze, draws her oriental dances and publishes the sheets at Leipzig; Alfred Richard Meyer prints the first monograph, a slim Berlin hymn titled simply Charlotte Bara. At twenty she is a documented style: the sunken knee the academies scold, the lifted palms, the face of quiet blessedness. The Städel will keep a drawing of the dancer; the archive of her body accumulates in other artists' hands, since her art itself vanishes each evening.
